name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Hollowbrook Farm by seven, after I've seen Robert off to his bowls or his allotment. It's the Pryce family's farm, sheep on the hill, about six hundred ewes, and oats and turnips on the lower fields for winter feed. I help with the flock, the feeding, the lambing in spring, and I keep the farm kitchen going at harvest. I've been there four years and I'm still the one they send for the easy jobs, which is fair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I raised four children and ran the church hall kitchen for twenty years, unpaid most of it. When the youngest left home, Huw Pryce, who sits two pews in front of us, said they were short of a pair of hands and would I like to try. My father kept sheep, so it wasn't all new. I don't have one of those smart phones and I've no wish for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there's a surprise, and thank goodness. I'd say it after the service over a cup of tea, and the men would nod. Most things that come out of the cities turn out to be less than they promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I go on as I am, which is all I want. I'm content with the work and the Pryces are good people. I don't want to learn new things at my age, I want to do the old things a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at all different. I'd go to Hollowbrook four days a week, help at lambing and do the harvest dinners. Robert and I would keep our savings where they are, with the building society, and I'd keep my old mobile phone in the kitchen drawer where it lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be glad to see some of the small things AI could do on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. The young Pryce boy, Rhys, has been talking about a collar for the sheep that tells you where they are on a phone. If a collar can find a lost ewe in the snow, I'm not against it. I just don't want to be the one carrying the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the farm work matters most to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lambing's my favourite. Three in the morning, a ewe in trouble, you get the lamb out and it shakes its head and bleats. No machine has ever felt what that feels like.

S0.say: I'd say there's a surprise, and thank goodness, over tea after the church service. Most things that come out of the cities turn out to be less than they promised.
S0.think: I go on as I am, which is all I want, with good people at a farm I'm content on. I don't want to learn new things at my age; I want to do the old things a bit better.
S0.do: Keeps working four days a week at the farm, helping at lambing and cooking the harvest dinners. Leaves savings with the building society and her old mobile phone in the kitchen drawer.
S0.quote: Three in the morning, a ewe in trouble, you get the lamb out and it shakes its head and bleats. No machine has ever felt what that feels like.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's faith and church community are the frame of her working life; she got her job through a fellow churchgoer. She's not against helpful gadgets as long as someone else carries them. Lambing is where her pride and feeling sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be careful what they let into their lives and their work. I'd say it at church and to the family. And I'd say the government should keep its nose out and let farmers decide for themselves, not tip money at the big tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry for the Pryces more than me. They're a family farm, three generations, and if the big farms down the valley get robots and sell lamb cheaper, the Pryces have to keep up or sell. And if they keep up, I'm the one they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and do my work as well as I can and see what the Pryces decide. I wouldn't go chasing a course, I'm 58 and slow on the new things. If they let me go, I'd go with no hard feelings, and Robert and I would be fine on what we've put by and his pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the year the auction mart prices dropped and nobody said anything at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the Pryces said they were thinking about robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray about it, honestly. That's not a figure of speech for me. And I'd talk to the minister, who's seen half the valley through foot-and-mouth and worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robert would say we'll manage, and we would. My son David would tell me to get a smart phone and learn it, and I'd tell him I've managed fifty-eight years without, thank you. We'd laugh about it, but he'd keep on.

S1.say: I'd say people should be careful what they let into their lives and work. The government should let farmers decide for themselves and not tip money at the big tech firms.
S1.think: I'd worry for the owners more than me: a three-generation family farm that has to keep up with cheaper robot lamb or sell. And if they keep up, I'm the one they don't need.
S1.do: Carries on and waits to see what the owners decide, without chasing any course. If let go, leaves without hard feelings, relying on savings and her husband's pension, and turns to prayer and her minister.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the year auction prices dropped and nobody spoke at dinner.
S1.quote: I'd pray about it, honestly. That's not a figure of speech for me.
S1.fieldNote: She blames big tech and government favour toward it, not the farmers. Her concern for the family farm comes before her own job. Her faith and her minister are her first support, not any official scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and it's going too fast for any decent person to keep up. I'd say it at church and to anyone. I'd say families and communities will pay the price while a few men in the cities count their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me. Not for the money, we've enough. For the valley. If robots run the farms, the young families go, the school closes, the chapel empties. I'd be watching the place I grew up in turn into somewhere I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit down with Robert and our savings, and make sure the house is safe and some money is there for the children. I'd tell Huw Pryce I'll go whenever they need me to, so he doesn't feel bad. And I'd put my time into the church and the young families, the food bank and the toddler group, because people will need each other more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep over it, not for me but for everyone round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short window change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away the time for a community to adjust. Farms change slowly, they always have, a field takes years to come right. Two years would be like a flood, it goes through and you clear up after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most afraid for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Ffion's husband, Owain, is a shepherd on a bigger farm. They've two little ones. If he's out, they'd have to move to the city for work, if there is any, and we'd lose them from the valley. That's what would keep me awake.

S2.say: I'd say this is wrong and too fast for any decent person to keep up. Families and communities will pay the price while a few men in the cities count their money.
S2.think: It frightens me, not for money but for the valley: young families leaving, the school closing, the chapel emptying. I'd watch the place I grew up in become somewhere I don't know.
S2.do: Checks the house and savings with her husband and sets money aside for the children. Tells the owner she'll go whenever needed, then puts her time into church, the food bank and the toddler group.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, not for herself but for everyone around her.
S2.quote: Farms change slowly, they always have, a field takes years to come right. Two years would be like a flood, it goes through and you clear up after.
S2.fieldNote: Her alarm is about her valley and way of life, not her income, which is secure. Her son-in-law's shepherding job makes the threat personal. She would answer it through church and family rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so families and churches had better start looking after each other now. I'd say the government shouldn't be throwing money around, but it should make the big companies pay their share. And I'd say I'm not learning to drive a robot, thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 63, and I'd have stopped by then, most likely. So it's less about me. It's still about Owain and the little ones, and the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hollowbrook as long as they wanted me. Robert and I would put a bit more aside so we could help Ffion and Owain if he lost his place. I'd talk to Ffion about whether they'd want to come and live nearer us, in the little house next door that's coming up for sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than with two years, but it'd be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really help them buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would, yes, if it came to it. It's got a good garden, and the little ones could come to us after school. That's how my mother did it, and her mother. Family first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you say to the Pryces?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd say they're good people. They'd do what they had to. I'd rather they kept the farm with robots than sold it to a company.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so families and churches had better start looking after each other now. Government shouldn't throw money around, but big companies should pay their share.
S3.think: I'd be 63 and likely stopped by then, so it's less about me. It's still about my son-in-law, the grandchildren and the valley.
S3.do: Keeps working at the farm as long as wanted and saves more with her husband to help her daughter's family. Talks with her daughter about buying the house next door so the grandchildren can come after school.
S3.feel: Anxious, less than with two years, but always there.
S3.quote: I'd rather they kept the farm with robots than sold it to a company.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she plans like her mother did: family close and money ready. She surprisingly accepts robots if they keep the family farm in the family. The government should make companies pay, but not hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families to prepare, and they should. I'd say the young should learn a trade, something with their hands, and stay close to home. And I'd say it won't be the end of the world, because the world has ended before and kept going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 68 and done. It's the grandchildren. What will they do, what will make them get up in the morning?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and stop at 62 or 63. I'd talk to the family about the house next door. I'd teach the grandchildren to lamb, if the Pryces would let them come, so they know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quieter way. More a sadness than a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach the grandchildren to lamb if robots will do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody ought to know how. Even if the robots do it all, if the power goes or the robot breaks, somebody should know how to turn a lamb. My father taught me when I was eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the grandchildren to hold on to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard to say. Prayer helps. And honest work, that's what I'd tell them, whatever form it takes.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families to prepare, and the young should learn a trade with their hands and stay close to home. The world has ended before and kept going.
S4.think: I'd be 68 and done, so it's about the grandchildren. What will make them get up in the morning?
S4.do: Carries on and stops work at 62 or 63. Talks with the family about the house next door and teaches her grandchildren to lamb at the farm.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a quieter way, more sadness than fear.
S4.quote: Even if the robots do it all, if the power goes or the robot breaks, somebody should know how to turn a lamb.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years her unease remains, because it's about meaning for the next generation rather than money. She wants old skills passed down as insurance. Faith and honest work are her answers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would take the valley apart before anyone could catch their breath. What would help is the big companies paying their way, and the money going to keep families on the land, not to people in offices, and churches and communities given room to look after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and people don't. But that's how most of us round here will get through it, whatever comes. I'm not worried about heaven. I'm worried about the school bus with nobody on it.

headlineQuote: I'm not worried about heaven. I'm worried about the school bus with nobody on it.
portrait: Beth Evans is 58 and came to farm work four years ago after raising four children and running her church hall kitchen; she helps with the sheep and lambing at Hollowbrook, a three-generation family hill farm owned by fellow churchgoers. She has no smartphone and no wish for one, and she's secure thanks to savings and her husband's pension. Her worry is never her own income but her valley: young families leaving, the school and chapel emptying. The two-year AGI picture alarms her, especially for her son-in-law, a shepherd with young children. She looks to faith, family and community, wants big companies to pay their share and would teach her grandchildren to lamb just in case.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take the valley apart before anyone could catch their breath.
whatWouldHelp: The big companies paying their way, with the money keeping families on the land, and churches and communities given room to look after their own.
